The beast's healed wound and borrowed throne parody the Lamb's death, resurrection and enthronement. The counterfeit always imitates.
The land beast has horns 'like a lamb' but speaks like a dragon: religion that looks like Christ but speaks accusation.
Forehead and hand are mind and works. The battle of the book is over what governs a person's thinking and doing.
666 is man's number, effort that never reaches God's seventh-day rest.
The Lamb was slain 'from the foundation of the world' (Revelation 13:8, as many translate it). The cross predates and outlasts every beast.
The three figures are read as James's three wisdoms that are not from above: earthly, soulish and demonic (James 3:15).
It rises from the restless sea, humanity unrenewed. It is the flesh in political form.
A counterfeit resurrection. The old system appears to recover, but only the Lamb truly rose.
Names written in the Lamb's book are secure. Identity rests on his slaying, not on the believer's performance.
Religion that resembles the Lamb but speaks like the dragon, accusing, controlling and demanding.
Humanity remaking God in its own image. It is the opposite of being conformed to the image of the Son (Romans 8:29).
A mind and works shaped by the flesh and fear. The counter is the Spirit's seal and a renewed mind.
Life as transaction. Grace stands outside that economy because it is freely given (Isaiah 55:1).
Six repeated three times is man's best effort, always short of the seventh-day rest.
13:1 Standing on the sand

The teaching notices that the sea-beast appears once John is standing on the sand of the sea (in the reading followed here). Sand is read through Solomon's 'largeness of heart like the sand on the seashore' as the wisdom of the earthly person, which later turned after other gods. From that standpoint the beast rises into view; from heaven it would not look the same.
13:2–4 The dragon gives the beast his throne

This view reads 'heaven' as whatever rules a person: whatever is obeyed becomes the throne over them. Either the Son sits on that throne within, or the dragon and the beast do. 'Who is like the beast?' shows that what a person follows becomes their god.
13:1, 11 Three beasts, three wisdoms

The teaching matches James's three kinds of wisdom that are not from above with the chapter's three figures: earthly (the beast from the earth), soulish or sensual (the beast from the sea) and demonic (the dragon). They act as one. Their opposite is the wisdom from above, pure, peaceable and full of mercy.
13:7–10 War on the saints

On this reading the beast can overcome saints because they are still earthly in some areas of life. It is 'those who dwell on the earth', a phrase the chapter keeps repeating, who worship it. The overcoming comes through the patience and faith of the saints.
13:11–14 Horns like a lamb, voice like a dragon

The second beast, later called the false prophet, is read as earthly wisdom that looks like the Lamb but speaks the dragon's language, a wolf in sheep's clothing. Its signs, even fire from heaven, impress but deceive.
13:14–15 The image and its breath

This view reads the image of the beast as a man-made picture of God carved in the mind: God in the image of man rather than man in the image of God. A Christ who comes to devour and destroy is given as an example of such an image. Once engraved it is 'given breath' and feels real, and the golden calf, hailed by the Lord's own name, is the pattern.
13:16–17 The mark as an engraving

The teaching connects the word 'mark' with Paul's phrase in Acts 17:29 for something 'shaped by art and man's devising'. The mark is that engraved false image ruling the forehead (thinking) and the right hand (authority and action), and it becomes the currency of everyday buying and selling. Against it God writes his own image, as he once engraved the tablets.
13:18 Here is wisdom: the number of a man

The chapter closes with a call for wisdom, and the beast's number is 'the number of a man'. This view takes it to mean that the beast is human wisdom and a human image of God. Christ is the reverse: God made man, not man made into a god.
The Lamb on Mount Zion, the eternal gospel and the harvest
The Lamb standing on Mount Zion with his people, who bear his name and his Father's on their foreheads. He is the Son of Man on the white cloud who reaps the harvest of the earth.

Straight after the beast's mark, John sees the Lamb on Mount Zion with the 144,000, who have his name and his Father's name written on their foreheads. The contrast is deliberate: two marks and two identities. They sing a new song only they can learn, follow the Lamb wherever he goes, and are called firstfruits. This view reads 'Mount Zion' through Hebrews 12:22, the heavenly Jerusalem that believers have already come to. Their 'virginity' and blamelessness describe undivided devotion to the Lamb, set against the harlot's mixture. It is not a moral achievement.

An angel then flies with the eternal gospel for every nation. Babylon's fall is announced, and a solemn warning is given against receiving the beast's mark. The chapter ends with two harvests. The Son of Man on a white cloud reaps the grain harvest, which this view reads as the fruit of the gospel gathered in. Then the vine of the earth is gathered and trodden in the winepress outside the city. This view reads that as the false vine of earthly life crushed, and notes that Christ himself suffered outside the city and trod the winepress alone. Even the warnings are held within the gospel: 'Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord, for they rest from their labours'.
Two marks side by side: the beast's (chapter 13) and the Lamb's and Father's name (chapter 14). Identity is the issue.
The new song can only be learned by the redeemed. It is the song of grace.
The eternal gospel goes to every nation before any harvest. Good news comes first.
'They rest from their labours' (Revelation 14:13) states the rest of those in Christ.
Two harvests: grain gathered (the fruit of the gospel) and the false vine crushed (the end of the old).
The believer's true standing is the heavenly Zion (Hebrews 12:22). It is already reached in Christ.
The Father's name on the mind is a new identity that answers the beast's mark.
A song of redemption that only the redeemed can learn. It is the song of grace.
Undivided devotion to the Lamb, the bride as opposed to the harlot's mixture.
Firstfruits promise a full harvest. Christ's people are the beginning of his new creation (James 1:18).
The good news is eternal and universal, and it is announced before the harvest.
Those in the Lord rest from their labours, the opposite of the beast-worshippers who have no rest.
The Son of Man gathers the fruit of the gospel. The seed that died bears much fruit.
The song of Moses and the Lamb: victory sung before the bowls

The Lamb whose song is joined to Moses' song. He is the true Exodus and the King of the nations, whose righteous acts have been revealed. He alone trod the winepress outside the city (Revelation 14:20; Isaiah 63:3).

Before the last plagues are poured out, John sees the victors standing beside a sea of glass mixed with fire. They hold harps and sing the song of Moses and the song of the Lamb. The scene recalls Israel on the far shore of the Red Sea after Egypt's army was overthrown. This view stresses the order. The victory song is sung before the bowls, because the outcome is already settled and the believer reads the judgments from the far shore.

The song itself says nothing about the singers' achievements. It is entirely about God: great and marvellous are his works, just and true are his ways, all nations will come and worship. The temple fills with smoke from God's glory, and no one can enter until the plagues are finished. This view reads that as the completion of God's work on the old order. It is something he does, and human effort contributes nothing to it.

This view also stresses that the bowls complete God's wrath rather than begin it. On this reading the scroll is the believer's inheritance: sealed, then read aloud in the trumpets, then made visible in the bowls. As in Egypt, the plagues fall on Pharaoh, on what enslaves, not on God's people. The teaching reads 'judgments' in 15:4 as 'righteous requirements' (as in Romans 8:4), fulfilled in those who walk by the Spirit, and that is why the nations come to worship.
The victory song comes before the bowls. Believers read judgment from the far shore of the Exodus.
The song of Moses and the song of the Lamb are one song. The Exodus is fulfilled in Christ's Passover.
The song is wholly God-centred and celebrates his works, not the victors' own.
'All nations will come and worship' sets a hopeful, universal horizon even in the context of judgment.
The bowls complete God's wrath rather than start it (Revelation 15:1). On this reading it began when Christ was confessed as Lord and the accuser was cast down.
'Judgments' in Revelation 15:4 is read as 'righteous requirements', as in Romans 8:4, fulfilled in those who walk by the Spirit.
The calm sea of chapter 4 now mixed with fire. Believers stand on it after passing through, like Israel beyond the Red Sea.
They overcame the beast, its image and its number by the Lamb, not by their own resistance.
The first Exodus and the final Exodus sung as one song. Christ is the Passover Lamb.
Christ reigns over the nations now. The bowls do not put his kingship in doubt.
The goal of judgment is worship and restoration, not mere destruction.
God alone completes this work, and no one enters to help. It is finished by him.
15:1 Wrath completed

The seven last plagues are those in which God's wrath 'is finished'. This view reads the bowls as completing, not starting, God's wrath against whatever holds a person captive. On this reading that wrath began when Christ was confessed as Lord and the accuser was cast down.
5–16 Seals, trumpets, bowls

On this reading the scroll is the believer's inheritance. The seals keep it closed, the trumpets open and read it as revelation, and the bowls make what was read visible in daily life. Knowing alone is not the goal; the bowls are the work of God becoming seen.
15:2–3 The song of Moses and the Lamb

The song recalls Israel's deliverance at the sea. This view reads the bowls through the plagues of Egypt, which fell on Pharaoh and not on Israel: on what enslaves, not on the enslaved. 'Great and marvellous are your works' marks the bowls as God's own work made visible.
15:4 Your righteous acts revealed

The teaching reads 'judgments' here as 'righteous requirements', comparing Romans 8:4, where the righteous requirement of the law is fulfilled in those who walk by the Spirit. The nations come to worship because something has been done to set them free.
14:19–20 The winepress outside the city

As background to the bowls, the vine of the earth is thrown into the winepress and trodden outside the city. This view reads it as the cross: Christ alone treading the winepress as in Isaiah 63, dealing with the bitter grapes of Isaiah's vineyard song. The day of vengeance ends in comfort for those who mourn.
The bowls poured out: 'It is done'

Christ is revealed in the cry 'It is done' from the throne, which echoes 'It is finished' from the cross. He is also the one who comes like a thief and blesses those who stay awake and keep their garments.

The seven bowls are poured out in quick succession. They mirror the trumpets but are now total rather than partial. Sores, the sea and rivers turning to blood, a scorching sun, darkness on the beast's throne, the Euphrates dried up and a great earthquake. Futurist readers see global catastrophe at the end of the tribulation. This view reads the bowls as the full exposure and end of the beast system. Everything the old order drank from turns to blood, its throne is plunged into darkness, and its subjects gnaw their tongues in pain yet still do not change their minds.

In the middle of the bowls Christ speaks directly: 'Behold, I am coming like a thief. Blessed is the one who stays awake and keeps his garments.' The believer's call is to stay alert and clothed in Christ's righteousness, not to stockpile or fear. At the seventh bowl a loud voice from the throne says 'It is done'. This view hears the cross in it: what was finished at Golgotha is here shown complete over the whole system of sin and death. Babylon splits in three, and every island and mountain flees. The old is not reformed. It is ended.

The teaching surveyed here reads each bowl as striking the old man and the beast system within, not people as such. The bowls fall on the earth, where the dragon was cast down. The sea turned to blood strikes the beast at its source, and the rivers recall the serpent's flood of words (12:15), so God heals the mouth as well as the heart. The people scorched are read as the old man, since every nation is still to come and worship (15:4). Romans 1:18 is read as wrath against the ungodliness of people, not against people themselves.
'It is done' (Revelation 16:17) is read as the echo of 'It is finished' (John 19:30). The bowls show the cross's verdict made complete.
The bowls fall on those who bear the beast's mark and worship its image. They are aimed at the beast system, not at the sealed.
Even total judgment does not produce repentance (Revelation 16:9, 11). Only grace changes the mind.
The beatitude in the middle of the bowls (Revelation 16:15) calls believers to wakefulness and to stay clothed in Christ.
Armageddon is gathered but never fought in this chapter. The outcome was settled before the armies assembled.
The people scorched (Revelation 16:8-9) are read as the old man. Wrath falls on the ungodliness of people, not on people themselves (Romans 1:18).
Bowls once held incense prayers (Revelation 5:8). Now they pour out the end of the old order.
The beast's kingdom is shown for what it is: darkness and a darkened understanding.
Pressure and pain do not renew the mind. Only the revelation of Christ does.
Unclean spirits from the mouths of dragon, beast and false prophet. Deception comes as words, and it is answered by the Word.
A call to stay awake in Christ and clothed in his garments. It is wakefulness, not fear.
The battle is gathered but never described. The victory was won at the cross.
The finished work spoken from the throne over the whole old order.
Babylon divided and collapsing. The system of self-effort cannot hold together.
16:1 Poured on the earth

The bowls are poured on the earth, where the dragon was cast down in chapter 12 and where the beast and Babylon hold sway. This view reads them as falling on what deceives the earthly, carnal mind, not on heaven and not on people as such.
16:2–3 Sores, and the sea as blood

The first bowl strikes those with the mark and the image, which this view reads as the earthly, soulish old self within the believer rather than a separate class of humanity. The second turns the sea to blood 'like that of a dead man', striking the beast at its source, the sea it rose from.
16:4–7 Rivers, springs and words

The third bowl falls on rivers and springs, which the teaching links with the flood from the serpent's mouth (12:15): streams of earthly wisdom and words. The angel of the waters and the altar answer that God's judgments are true and righteous. On this reading God heals not only heart and mind but also the mouth.
16:8–9 The 'men' who are scorched

The teaching reads the people scorched by the sun as the old man, not people as such. Otherwise, it argues, every nation could not come and worship (15:4) and every knee bow. Wrath is revealed against the ungodliness and unrighteousness of people rather than against people themselves.
16:13–14 Unclean spirits from three mouths
The frog-like spirits come out of the mouths of the dragon, the beast and the false prophet. This view reads them as words of earthly wisdom: spiritual messages, not creatures from science fiction.
16:17–19 'It is done' and Babylon divided

The seventh bowl's cry is heard as the cry of the cross, 'It is finished'. Babylon is remembered and falls, and this view reads her fall as releasing the nations to come out and worship. Chapters 17 and 18 are read as unfolding inside this last bowl.
The harlot on the beast: religion of mixture exposed
The Lamb who conquers because he is Lord of lords and King of kings, with those who are called, chosen and faithful.

An angel takes John into the wilderness 'in the Spirit' to show him the great harlot seated on many waters and riding a scarlet beast. She is dressed in purple and scarlet, gold and pearls, and holds a golden cup full of abominations. On her forehead is a name: Babylon the Great, mother of harlots. Interpreters have identified her with Rome, apostate Jerusalem, a future world religion or a corrupt church. This view keeps the historical candidates in mind but reads her as a spiritual pattern: the religion of mixture, which has a form of relationship with God while giving itself to the world's wealth and power. She rides the beast, so religion is carried along by worldly power.

Her name is on her forehead, so she is a mind with a counterfeit identity, the harlot's mark answering the bride's name. She is drunk with the blood of the saints, which is religion that persecutes the life of the Spirit. The chapter's outcome is striking. The beast and its horns come to hate the harlot and destroy her, because the system turns on itself. Meanwhile the Lamb conquers because of who he is: Lord of lords and King of kings. His people with him are called, chosen and faithful, and every one of those words describes grace.
John must be carried 'in the Spirit' to see the harlot rightly. Spiritual perception is needed to discern counterfeit religion.
The harlot is richly dressed in what she has bought. The bride is given fine linen.
The name on her forehead is a counterfeit identity, set against the Lamb's name on his people's foreheads.
The beast destroys the harlot. Systems of flesh and self-effort turn on themselves.
The Lamb conquers by who he is: 'called, chosen and faithful' describes the result of grace.
Unfaithful devotion: a form of relationship with God while loving other things. She is the bride's counterfeit.
Religion riding on worldly power, carried by the flesh's systems.
Outward splendour bought by trade. It is the opposite of the bride's given linen.
A beautiful vessel full of impurity, religious appearance with mixture inside (Matthew 23:25).
Her mind bears a false identity, set against the Father's name on the bride's forehead.
The book calls for a discerning mind, a renewed understanding rather than a code to crack.
The Lamb conquers by who he is. It is victory from identity.
The old system consumes itself. What is built on the flesh cannot stand.
Babylon fallen: come out of her

Christ is revealed as the one who calls his people out, as the true merchant who sells gold without price, and as the lamp and bridegroom whose voice will never again be heard in Babylon because it belongs to the New Jerusalem. He is also the 'another angel' of 18:1, the Lord as Spirit, whose glory lights the earth with revelation.

A glorious angel lights the earth and cries 'Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great'. Then another voice says 'Come out of her, my people'. This view takes that call as the centre of the chapter. Coming out of Babylon is not mainly a geographical move or a withdrawal from society. It is a departure in mind and heart from the system of mixture, self-exaltation and trade in souls. Babylon says in her heart 'I sit as a queen and will never see mourning'. That is self-sufficiency again, and it falls in a single hour.

The long list of cargo, from gold, silver and fine linen down to cattle, sheep, horses and chariots, ends with 'slaves, that is, human souls'. This view reads the list as Babylon's real business: the commerce of the soul, a religious and economic system that buys and sells people and keeps them labouring for what does not satisfy. The kings and merchants lament from a distance, but heaven rejoices. The millstone thrown into the sea and the silence of the city's music, crafts, lamps and wedding voices show its total end. The lamp and the voice of the bridegroom and bride are not lost. They move to the other city.

The teaching surveyed here reads the angel who lights the earth as Christ himself, descending as Spirit into the parts of the soul not yet enlightened. Babylon is a mystery, and only revelation exposes it. Distinctively, it reads Babylon as the man-made, institutional religious system, fallen from grace into law-keeping and human doctrine, which looks exactly like the bride from outside (17:4; 21:18-21). The order is revelation, recognition, then departure. God calls his people out before he brings the system down, and he judges the system, not the people. The teaching applies this to oneself first.
'Come out of her' is a call to the mind and heart. The answer to Babylon is departure, not fear of her.
The cargo list ends with human souls. Babylon's real trade is people.
Babylon falls in one hour. What is built without God has no foundation.
Heaven rejoices over her fall. The end of the old system is good news.
The bridegroom's and bride's voices fall silent in Babylon because the wedding belongs to the New Jerusalem.
'Another angel' (Revelation 18:1) is read as Christ himself as Spirit, lighting the soul with revelation. No one can leave a mystery they cannot see.
Light exposes Babylon. Revelation brings the old system's fall.
Its fall is announced as already done, echoing Isaiah 21:9.
Leave the system of mixture and self-effort in mind and heart (2 Corinthians 6:17).
Self-sufficiency, the Laodicean boast enlarged into a city.
Everything traded, ending in souls. It is the economy of earning.
Babylon's real commerce is the human soul. Christ redeems the soul without price.
A total and final end, thrown into the restless sea from which the beast came.
The lamp and the wedding leave Babylon and are found in the city whose lamp is the Lamb.
18:1 Another angel

'Another' is read as the same Lord in another form or administration, just as Jesus promised 'another Helper' and Paul wrote that 'the Lord is the Spirit'. Coming down from heaven with great authority, this angel is taken to be Christ himself as Spirit.
18:1 The earth lit with his glory

On this reading Christ descends from the 'heaven' of the believer's spirit into the 'earth' of a soul not yet enlightened. The light is revelation, the eyes of the heart enlightened, and revelation is what a 'mystery' such as Babylon requires.
18:2 Fallen, fallen

This view reads the cry as an unveiling of Babylon's existing condition rather than news of a fresh event: she has fallen from grace by seeking righteousness through law. Her dens of demons and unclean birds are read as false doctrines and spirits of error.
17:4–5 with 21:18–21 Two women, one appearance

Distinctively, this teaching reads Babylon as the man-made, institutional religious system, in contrast to the church Christ builds by revelation. Harlot and bride wear the same gold, precious stones and pearls, so they cannot be told apart from outside. She is 'mother of harlots' because the drift began early, as Paul's 'so soon' to the Galatians shows.
18:4 Come out of her, my people

The sequence is revelation (verse 1), recognition (verse 2), then departure (verse 4): no one can leave a mystery they cannot see. God calls his people out before the system falls, and he judges the system, not the people. The teaching insists the call is applied to oneself, not used to judge other believers.
18:21 and Jeremiah 51 The destroying wind and the stone

The chapter draws heavily on Jeremiah 51. This view reads the 'destroying wind' and the stirred-up spirit of the kings of the Medes as the Spirit at work through those joined to the Lord. The scroll weighted with a stone and sunk in the Euphrates is the pattern for the millstone thrown into the sea.
11:13 and 14:1–4 Firstfruits, then the harvest

The tenth of the city that falls in chapter 11 is read as a tithe, recalling Abraham's tenth to Melchizedek, and the firstfruits on Mount Zion as the first to come out. Firstfruits imply a full harvest still to be gathered out of Babylon, so those who have come out are there to help others out, not to boast.
The marriage of the Lamb and the Word on the white horse

The Bridegroom whose marriage has come, Faithful and True, the Word of God whose robe is dipped in blood. He conquers by the sword from his mouth and bears the name King of kings and Lord of lords. He is the Bridegroom who will not force a bride, whose own righteous act is the linen she is given.

Heaven bursts into Hallelujah because the harlot is judged and the marriage of the Lamb has come. The two women of the book meet their ends: the harlot falls and the bride stands ready. Her fine linen, bright and clean, was 'given to her'. The text identifies it as the righteous acts of the saints, and this view reads those acts as the fruit of grace rather than the price of admission. 'Blessed are those invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb.' This view treats the marriage as the goal of the whole book and of the cross: union with Christ.

Then heaven opens and a rider on a white horse appears, called Faithful and True, the Word of God. Many readers see the second coming here. Most in this view also affirm a future return, but they stress that this rider conquers in the way the Lamb conquers. His robe is dipped in blood before any battle, and that is his own blood. The only weapon named comes from his mouth. His armies wear fine linen and are never shown fighting. The beast and the false prophet are captured, and the rest are slain by the sword of his mouth. On this reading the Word ends the old order, and the opposite supper, the birds' feast, shows what becomes of everything that exalted itself against him.

The teaching surveyed here reads the chapter as the high point of a love story that began with Adam and Eve. The Lamb does not force a bride who does not love him; the seals, trumpets and bowls were his work of washing her until his love reached her heart. Her linen is his 'righteous act' given to her (Romans 5:18), the reverse of the fig leaves sewn in Eden. Once clothed she rides in his army, and the war of 19:11-21 is read as the Word clearing away what remains of the flesh. The church that was one spirit with the Lord in chapter 1 is here brought to the 'one flesh' of the marriage.
Two women and two suppers. The harlot's judgment and the bride's wedding belong together in one chapter.
The bride's linen is 'given', so her righteousness is received as a gift and expressed in life.
The rider's robe is dipped in blood before the battle. It is the blood of the cross, not of his enemies.
The only weapon is the sword from his mouth: Christ conquers by his word.
The testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy (Revelation 19:10). All true prophecy bears witness to him.
The bride's linen is read as the Bridegroom's 'righteous act' given to her (Romans 5:18), the reverse of Eden's fig leaves.
The goal of the book and of the cross: union with Christ.
Given to her to wear. Righteousness is received first and then lived out.
The principle behind the whole reading: prophecy exists to bear witness to Jesus.
Christ conquering by his word and by the way of the Lamb. Most proponents also see in him the hope of his appearing.
The blood is on the robe before the fight, so it is his own: the cross is his victory.
His name is the Word. He wins by speaking.
The word that judges thoughts and frees captives. It is his only weapon.
The opposite supper: the end of everything that exalted itself, set against the marriage feast.
19:1–2 One judgment, two outcomes

Heaven's Hallelujah celebrates judgments that are true and righteous. This view reads one judgment working two ways: the harlot is put away and the bride is made ready. Every judgment aims at salvation and at God's glory being seen on earth.
19:7 The bride has made herself ready

On this reading the Lamb does not force a bride who does not love him. Everything up to chapter 19, the seals, trumpets and bowls, is his work of washing the church until his love, shown long ago at the cross, reaches her heart and she receives it. Scripture opens with a wedding in Eden and closes with this one.
19:8 Fine linen: the righteous act given

'It was granted to her' marks the linen as a gift. The teaching reads 'the righteous acts of the saints' as the holy righteous act of the Bridegroom, comparing 'one man's righteous act' in Romans 5:18, rather than the bride's religious performance. It is the reverse of the fig leaves Adam and Eve sewed, and recalls the garments God made for them himself.
19:11–13 The rider called the Word of God

After the bride is ready there is war again. This view reads the rider, Faithful and True, whose name is the Word of God, as the Word himself dealing with the last remnants of Adamic carnality in his people. His robe is dipped in blood before any battle.
19:14 Armies in fine linen

The armies wear the same linen the bride has just received. On this reading, once the bride is ready she rides in his army: no longer captive in Babylon but on the Bridegroom's side against what remains of the flesh.
19:15, 21 The sword from his mouth

Every enemy falls to the sword of his mouth, which this view reads as the Word destroying another 'word' within: God's wisdom ends human wisdom and truth ends the lie. The teaching treats this cleansing as part of the marriage supper, the bride yielding to her husband's love and putting away what is left of the harlot.
Chapters 1 and 19 One spirit, then one flesh

This view notes that Ephesians speaks of 'one flesh', not 'one spirit'. It reads the believer as first one spirit with the Lord and then brought to oneness in the flesh, which it connects with the lowly body being changed to be like his glorious body. Revelation 1 shows the church one in spirit, and chapter 19 the union made complete.
The strong man bound: reigning in life

Christ is revealed as the one who binds the strong man, the resurrection and the life, the King with whom his people reign, and the Judge on the great white throne before whom death and Hades are destroyed. He is also the true Head and Husband of the soul, and himself the book of life.
